entries.1:1: Paul introduces himself as God's servant and Jesus' appointed messenger, working for the faith of God's people and for true knowledge of what pleases God. It reminds the reader that serving God means both trusting him and learning what is true.
entries.1:2: Paul's work rests on the hope of eternal life, which God promised long ago and cannot lie about. The reader can trust that this hope is solid because it depends on God's character, not on circumstances.
entries.1:3: At the right time God made his message clear through the good news, and Paul was given the job of announcing it by God's command. It shows that sharing God's message is a task God himself assigns.
entries.1:4: Paul writes to Titus as a genuine son in the faith they share, wishing him grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus. It shows the warmth and family bond between those who follow Jesus.
entries.1:5: Paul left Titus in Crete to finish organizing the work and to appoint leaders for the churches in each town, just as Paul had instructed. It shows that good order and responsible leadership matter in the church.
entries.1:6: Leaders must have a good reputation, be faithful in marriage, and have children who believe and are not wild or out of control. It means a leader's home life is part of what qualifies them to lead.
entries.1:7: A church leader, as God's manager, must be blameless—not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not violent, and not greedy for money. It means leaders are accountable to God for how they treat people and handle money.
entries.1:8: Instead, a leader should welcome guests, love what is good, be sensible, fair, holy, and self-controlled. It means leadership is shown in everyday character, not just in words.
entries.1:9: A leader must hold firmly to the true teaching so he can encourage others with sound instruction and correct those who argue against it. It means knowing the truth well enough to help and defend others.
entries.1:10: Many people, especially some from a Jewish background, are rebellious, talk nonsense, and teach what is false. It warns the reader that not everyone who talks about God is teaching the truth.
entries.1:11: These false teachers upset whole families and teach wrong things for money, so they must be silenced. It means greed-driven false teaching does real damage and needs to be stopped.
entries.1:12: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet who described his own people as liars, dangerous, lazy, and greedy. It shows that even their own writers admitted the problem was real.
entries.1:13: Paul says this description is accurate, so Titus should correct them firmly so they can return to the true faith. It means loving correction can help people get back on track.
entries.1:14: They should stop paying attention to Jewish myths and to rules made by people who reject the truth. It means believers should not be led astray by made-up stories or human regulations.
entries.1:15: To those who are pure, everything is pure, but to those who are corrupt and unbelieving, nothing is pure—their minds and consciences are stained. It means what we are inside shapes how we see everything else.
entries.1:16: They claim to know God, but their actions deny him; they are detestable, disobedient, and useless for any good work. It means claiming faith means nothing if your life doesn't back it up.
entries.2:1: Paul tells Titus that what he teaches must match the healthy, correct message about Jesus. For the reader, it means our words about God should line up with the truth we've been taught.
entries.2:2: Older men should be calm, self-controlled, sensible, and strong in faith, love, and patience. For the reader, it's a picture of how maturity in years should show itself in steady, trustworthy character.
entries.2:3: Older women should live in a way that earns respect, avoid gossip and heavy drinking, and teach what is good. For the reader, it means the example older believers set really matters.
entries.2:4: These older women are to help younger women learn to love their husbands and children. For the reader, it shows that practical, everyday love in the home is something worth teaching and passing on.
entries.2:5: Younger women should be sensible, pure, kind, busy caring for their homes, and respectful toward their husbands, so God's message isn't discredited. For the reader, it means how we live at home can either honor or harm the reputation of God's word.
entries.2:6: Titus is told to urge young men to be sensible and serious-minded. For the reader, it's a call to take life seriously and make wise choices.
entries.2:7: Titus himself must be a model of good deeds, with teaching that is pure and behavior that is serious. For the reader, it means example speaks as loudly as words.
entries.2:8: His words should be sound and beyond criticism, so opponents have nothing bad to say about us. For the reader, it means living and speaking honestly can silence unfair criticism.
entries.2:9: Servants should submit to their masters, aim to please them, and not argue back. For the reader, it means doing your work well and respectfully, even when it's hard.
entries.2:10: They should not steal but show themselves fully trustworthy, so their conduct makes the teaching about God attractive. For the reader, it means honesty at work can point people toward God.
entries.2:11: God's grace has appeared, bringing salvation to all people. For the reader, it means salvation is a free gift from God offered to everyone.
entries.2:12: That grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness and worldly desires and to live wisely, rightly, and godly in this present life. For the reader, it means grace doesn't just save us; it also trains us how to live now.
entries.2:13: We are waiting with hope for the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ. For the reader, it means our hope is fixed on Jesus' return, which gives us reason to keep going.
entries.2:14: Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to make us a people who are his own, eager to do good. For the reader, it means Jesus' sacrifice both frees us from sin and makes us eager to do what is right.
entries.2:15: Titus should teach these things, encourage people, and correct them with full authority, and no one should look down on him. For the reader, it means sound teaching should be taught clearly and taken seriously.
entries.3:1: Christians should respect those in authority, obey the law, and be eager to do good. This means the way you treat government and leaders should reflect your faith.
entries.3:2: Don't speak badly about anyone, avoid quarrels, be considerate, and treat everyone gently. Your everyday dealings with people should be marked by kindness rather than conflict.
entries.3:3: Before we knew God, we too were foolish, stubborn, and slaves to our desires, living in envy and hatred. Remembering this should make you humble toward others instead of looking down on them.
entries.3:4: God our Savior showed his kindness and love for people by stepping in to help us. His goodness toward us was not something we earned but something he chose to show.
entries.3:5: He saved us not because of good things we did but because of his mercy, through a cleansing new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. Your salvation rests on God's kindness, not on your own record.
entries.3:6: God poured out the Holy Spirit on us generously through Jesus Christ our Savior. The new life you have comes as a gift from God through Jesus.
entries.3:7: Because God put us right with himself by his grace, we now have the hope of eternal life as our inheritance. You can live with confidence that your future with God is secure.
entries.3:8: This teaching is trustworthy, and Titus should insist on it so believers will devote themselves to good works. What you believe should show up in the good you actually do for others.
entries.3:9: Stay away from pointless debates, genealogies, and arguments about the law, because they waste time and lead nowhere. Don't get pulled into quarrels that don't help anyone grow.
entries.3:10: If someone keeps pushing divisive false teaching after being warned twice, have nothing more to do with them. Protecting the church sometimes means limiting contact with those who keep causing division.
entries.3:11: Such a person is clearly twisted and keeps sinning, and their own conduct condemns them. Their stubbornness shows the problem is with them, not with the truth.
entries.3:12: When Paul sends Artemas or Tychicus, Titus should make every effort to join him at Nicopolis, where Paul plans to spend the winter. Practical plans and timing matter in serving God too.
entries.3:13: Help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way and make sure they have everything they need. Supporting traveling workers is a real way to serve the mission.
entries.3:14: Our people should keep doing good works to meet real needs, so their lives produce something worthwhile. Faith that never helps anyone is fruitless, so put your energy into useful good.
entries.3:15: Everyone with Paul sends greetings, and he asks Titus to greet the friends in the faith, closing with a wish for grace on all. Christian friendship and encouragement are worth passing on.
